source.title: Increasing Both Batch Size and Learning Rate Accelerates Stochastic Gradient Descent

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendices; no material truncation or garbling noted.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares batch-size and learning-rate schedules and reports test accuracy, but its main measure is empirical-loss gradient norm rather than the training–test error gap.
record.gate_note: The paper’s main convergence results concern the full gradient norm of empirical loss. Prior-work results cited in the introduction and figures without a textual test-accuracy comparison are not extracted as findings. Test-accuracy claims are extracted only where the text describes them.
record.test_reason: The reported textual comparisons concern optimization and accuracy under joint batch-size and learning-rate schedules. They do not establish a large-batch held-out penalty or its removal relative to a smaller-batch baseline. The supplied figure text contains axes and legends but does not preserve readable accuracy differences between curves.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate, with the qualification that convergence and acceleration concern the expected full gradient norm of empirical loss. The authors support their analyses experimentally and acknowledge limited model and dataset coverage; they do not conclude that a large-batch generalization penalty has been established or eliminated.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes and compares SGD batch-size and learning-rate schedules, measuring empirical-loss gradient norms and also reporting test accuracy; it does not reproduce the original large-batch generalization-gap method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported test-accuracy outcome varies with batch growth factor and learning-rate schedule; the text says δ = 3, 4 outperform δ = 2 on CIFAR100 for the reported test-accuracy criterion.

fits_no_version.finding: On ResNet-18/CIFAR100, the authors report higher test accuracy for the modified δ = 3 and 4 schedules than for δ = 2, while batch-size and learning-rate trajectories change together.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Joint batch-size and learning-rate schedule design affects held-out accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: The theoretical and principal experimental outcomes concern convergence measured by the full gradient norm of empirical loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing batch sizes together with increasing or warm-up learning rates can accelerate SGD convergence to stationary points under the stated assumptions.

record.problems: The authors state that the numbers of models and datasets in the experiments were limited. Most test-accuracy results are presented in figures without numerical values or textual comparisons; the reported test-accuracy text does not isolate batch size from learning-rate schedule.
record.rows_left_out: Gradient-norm and training-loss rows were omitted because they do not measure the training–test error gap or the test-accuracy outcome named by V5. Other figure-only test-accuracy comparisons in Figures 1, 3–4, 8–21 were not extracted because the text gives no distinct result for them; Figure 7 is retained as an explicitly evaluated setting.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed to interpolate.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
An identifiable held-out penalty from larger batches at fixed epochs, and whether recipe changes remove that penalty relative to smaller batches; workload thresholds and language-model results.
Effects of adding or removing dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The existing V5 limits_scope label should be removed: high accuracy alone does not demonstrate a qualification of V5. Cross-figure constant-versus-increasing-batch accuracy comparisons could potentially bear on V5, but their curve values are unreadable here and the record already declares those figure-only results omitted.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum methods.

No fixed batch-size comparison specifically isolates the effect of a larger batch; results concern increasing-batch schedules. Language models, workload-dependent thresholds, and some cited recipe adjustments are not tested.

rows.subject: ResNet-18 on CIFAR100
rows.operation_detail: Compared constant batch size with doubly increasing batch size every 30 epochs under constant, cosine, linear, and polynomial learning-rate schedules.

conditions.value: constant versus doubly increasing every 30 epochs from b0 = 23

rows.value: Constant LR and Cosine LR were compatible with increasing batch size; using Constant LR performed well (test accuracy shown in Figure 2(d)).
rows.uncertainty: The solid line represents the mean and the shaded area the maximum and minimum over three runs.
rows.note: The text does not state a numerical accuracy difference or directly compare the increasing-batch schedules’ test accuracy with a constant-batch baseline.
rows.check: Figure 2 compares learning-rate schedules under the same increasing-batch schedule, not constant versus increasing batch size. The initial batch size is 2^3 = 8. The qualitative statement that constant learning rate performed well does not establish V5's batch-size penalty or recovery.

rows.subject: ResNet-18 on CIFAR100
rows.operation_detail: Compared batch-size and learning-rate schedules with increasing batch size and increasing learning rate, varying the batch growth factor.
rows.value: δ = 3, 4 was better than δ = 2 in the sense of minimizing empirical loss and achieving high test accuracy.
rows.uncertainty: The solid line represents the mean and the shaded area the maximum and minimum over three runs.
rows.note: The text reports a qualitative advantage for δ = 3, 4; it does not give test-accuracy values or compare with constant batch size.
rows.check: The stated accuracy advantage is correctly attributed, but 'partial' is not warranted for V5. These are modified schedules sharing batch-size endpoints of 8 and 4096 and learning-rate endpoints of 0.1 and 0.2. Larger δ does not mean uniformly larger batches; both schedule shapes change. This is a schedule-performance comparison without a demonstrated large-batch penalty or recovery.

rows.subject: ResNet-34 on ImageNet
rows.operation_detail: Trained with increasing batch sizes and warm-up decaying learning rates.

conditions.value: warm-up constant or warm-up cosine; ηmax = 1.0

rows.uncertainty: The solid line represents the mean and the shaded area the maximum and minimum over three runs.
rows.note: The appendix describes the figure as evaluating Case (iv) but gives no textual test-accuracy comparison.
rows.check: Figure 7 compares warm-up constant and warm-up cosine learning rates under the same increasing-batch schedule. It supplies no smaller-batch control, and accuracy differences cannot be read from the supplied text.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: ResNet-18 on CIFAR100; increasing batch schedules with altered learning-rate schedules
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that schedules using increasing batch sizes with learning-rate changes can achieve high test accuracy, and that δ = 3, 4 outperformed δ = 2 on that measure; these results do not isolate a general penalty from larger batches (R1, R2).
